lines.text: In 1999, three letters could make a stock jump: dot-com.
Then the floor fell out. The warning sign? A sock puppet.
Investors threw money at internet companies with little or no profit.
Profits? Not the question. Yet.
Proof? November 1998: the globe dot-com rose about 606 percent. On day one.
And in 1999 alone, the Nasdaq climbed about 85%.
Now, about that sock puppet. Meet Pets dot-com.
It sold pet food for less than it paid for it,
then shipped those heavy bags for free.
Lose money on the food. Pay to ship it. Repeat.
But it had the famous sock puppet, and a Super Bowl ad.
February 2000: it went public at $11 a share.
Weeks later, on March 10, the Nasdaq peaked above five thousand.
Then the music stopped.
Why? In under a year, the Fed raised interest rates six times.
Cheap money dried up.
And then came the yet. Investors asked one question: where are the profits?
Pets dot-com shut down that November, nine months after going public.
Webvan, the grocery delivery startup? Bankrupt in July 2001.
Even Amazon's stock fell more than 90%. Hold that thought.
In October 2002, the Nasdaq hit bottom: down about 78%.
How long to climb back above the old peak? Fifteen years. April 2015.
But the internet didn't die. The hype did.
And Amazon, the one that fell more than 90%? It became a giant.
So when everyone says this time is different, remember the sock puppet. Follow, and you'll spot the next bubble.
